newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia extradition bill clears latest hurdle.
newsitem.headline: Colombia extradition bill clears latest hurdle.

text.p: A bill to lift Colombia's six-year-old ban on the extradition of drug traffickers and other criminals edged closer to becoming law after a rocky debate in the lower house of Congress on Thursday.
The proposal, approved by 97-46 majority, revived government hopes of extradition with partial retroactivity but is still so watered down as to be virtually useless, critics say.

The bill has now cleared its final hurdle in the current session of Congress but must survive a further four debates in the next session of Congress, beginning July 20, if it is to make its way on to the statute books by the end of the year.
"This is a triumph for the country. Now we can send this project into the next session of Congress where it can receive full debate," Justice Minister Almabeatriz Rengifo said.

The vote in the Chamber of Representatives, at the end of almost nine hours of debate, opened the way to sending Colombians abroad to stand trial for crimes committed from the date when Colombia first signed a treaty with the country requesting extradition.
The Colombia-U.S. treaty dates back to 1979 but the partial retroactivity clause seems unlikely to impress U.S. anti-drug officials who have been pushing for an unconditional extradition agreement.
The bill, if it survives in its present form, would still ban extradition if the accused faced stiffer penalties abroad than under Colombia's notoriously lenient justice system.

Under tougher Colombian laws introduced at the end of last year, drug traffickers now face a maximum 60-year prison term. But in the United States, those convicted of similar crimes face multiple life sentences behind bars.
In its latest weekly bulletin, investment analysts Santander Investment gave a cool reaction to the extradition bill.

"The White House will not be satisfied until it sees top Colombian drug barons behind bars in the United States. As it stands the legislation would not lead to that...But we believe U.S. annoyance at any lack of progress would be soothed by the prospect of a new Administration next year."
Despite the potential shortfalls in the current bill, Foreign Relations Minister Maria Emma Mejia welcomed the vote.
"This shows the courage and commitment of Colombia," she told reporters. "It shows that if the executive and legislative branch of government work together we can defeat crime in our country."
During the debate, legislator Ingrid Betancur suggested Colombia's drug mobs had been fortified because of state complicity.

"Organized crime would not have the strength it does if there was not complicity at all levels of the state...the police, military and the presidency," she said, in barbed reference to the allegations that President Ernesto Samper financed his 1994 election campaign with millions of dollars in donations from the powerful Cali drug cartel.
